extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, patent litigators, and law students studying equity practice in U.S. federal courts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on drafting and defending bills (complaints), answers, amendments, interrogatories, affidavits, and bills of particulars in equity suits for patent cases under the pre- and post-1913 Equity Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer for relief: both special and general
rubrics_metrics.description: The prayer for relief should be both special and general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The special part should ask for a preliminary injunction, and for a permanent injunction, and for an account of the defendant's profits, and for an assessment of the complainant's damages, and for an increase of those damages, and for costs. The prayer for general relief should be in the ordinary form of prayers of that kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogating part: purpose and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The interrogating part of the bill was designed to secure from the defendant such admissions or statements as would obviate the necessity for evidence to support allegations of the bill relating to his doings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the formal interrogating part was abolished, its purpose is effected by filing specific interrogatories separately. The character, but not extent, of the defendant's doings could be the subject of interrogation; e.g., if infringement denied, defendant cannot be compelled to state how many infringing articles he has made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogatories: form and numbering (historical practice still relevant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an interrogating part contained more than one interrogatory, the interrogatories were required to be divided from each other, consecutively numbered, and a note required at the foot of the bill specifying which of those numbered interrogatories each defendant was required to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although practice changed, principles of clear numbering and specifying which defendant answers which interrogatory remain relevant when ordering interrogatories separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of waived oath on interrogatory answers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the complainant in his bill waived the oath which otherwise the defendant was entitled to make to his answer, or required such an oath only to certain specified interrogatories, the defendant's answer though under oath was not evidence in his favor on any point not covered by such specified interrogatories, unless the case was heard on bill and answer only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a general verification when you intend answers to serve as evidence on specific points; clearly delineate which interrogatories are sworn to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer for process: historic requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The prayer for process formerly had to contain the names of all the defendants mentioned in the introductory part of the bill and state if any were minors or under guardianship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No mention of these specific requirements in the 1913 rules, but be mindful of requirements in local practice or statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signing the bill
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill must be signed by one or more solicitors of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formerly the signature of 'counsel' was required; ensure proper counsel/solicitor of record signature as required by court rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification required for preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: An oath of the truth of the bill must be appended if it prays for a preliminary injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The oath must be made by the complainant or someone having knowledge of the facts upon which the application is based. For corporations, an officer who knows may verify, or if none knows, an agent or attorney who does. Positive oaths must be based on positive knowledge; where affiant only has information and belief, supplement with affidavits of persons with direct knowledge and expert affidavits comparing defendant's doings to the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of oath: specificity required
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not sufficient for the oath to state that the material averments of the bill are true or that those allegations true which render an injunction necessary; such forms leave uncertainty which allegations the affiant had in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oath should clearly discriminate between facts affirmatively known and those alleged on information and belief; identify which allegations are sworn positively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits: who may take them
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits to bills and other affidavits in civil causes in U.S. district courts may be taken before a commissioner of the District Court or before any notary public of the States, Territories, or District of Columbia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure affidavits are sworn before an authorized official per local practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill to perpetuate testimony vs. bill to establish non-infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill to perpetuate testimony tending to show a particular patent to be void may be filed and prosecuted in any U.S. District Court; but a bill brought to establish non-infringement of a particular patent by the complainant will not be entertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the bill-to-perpetuate-testimony device for attacks on validity, but not as a vehicle to seek a declaratory ruling of non-infringement by the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity will not restrain actions in other courts
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of equity will not restrain an action brought, or to be brought, in another court for infringement of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not seek equitable restraint of parallel proceedings in other courts; pursue appropriate remedies in the forum where action lies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on combining patent and pre-patent unfair competition claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill cannot be partly based on a patent and partly on unfair competition before the patent was in existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, a bill may properly pray that the defendant be restrained both from infringing a patent and from applying the designating name of the patented article to a spurious imitation while the patent is in force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity jurisdiction to restrain publications (free speech concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have considered requests to restrain patentees or alleged infringers from publishing statements favorable or unfavorable; most courts denied such applications, but a few granted them where the statements were not believed to be true by those who made them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the tension between equitable relief and freedom of speech; Supreme Court decisions have limited equity's jurisdiction to abridge freedom of the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments before response: as of course
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to bills may be made as a matter of course, and without costs, at any time before the defendant has responded thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If amendment is filed after any copy has issued from the clerk's office, the plaintiff must at his own cost furnish to opposing solicitors copies of the amended bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments after answer or hearing: court discretion and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: After an answer is put in, the complainant may obtain an order to amend his bill upon payment of costs or not, as the judge may direct; the court may at any time permit amendments in furtherance of justice on such terms as just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments at or after hearing are discretionary; precedents show amendments after hearing allowed only where bill defective in proper parties, prayer for relief, omission or misstatement of some fact connected with the substance but not the substance itself, or necessary to meet new matter in the answer. If litigation proceeded as if amendment existed, court will allow post-hearing amendment to conform pleadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a bill needs amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill needs amendment when the defendant's demurrer, plea, or answer points out a material fault, or when complainant discovers a material error or omission which may be cured, or when defendant's answer contains statements requiring pleading by way of confession and avoidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under modern Equity Rules replications have been abolished; plead by amended bill or answer as appropriate; consider whether issue should be raised by motion to dismiss or in the answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of demurrers and pleas (Equity Rule 29)
rubrics_metrics.description: By Rule 29 demurrers and pleas are abolished: every defence in point of law arising upon the face of the bill which might heretofore have been made by demurrer or plea shall be made by motion to dismiss or in the answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defences formerly presentable by plea in bar or abatement shall be made in the answer and may be separately heard before trial at the court's discretion. If defendant moves to dismiss, motion may be set down on five days' notice; if denied, answer must be filed within five days or decree pro confesso entered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of abolition: answer and motion to dismiss central
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of Rule 29 is to leave the answer as the means of defence against all matters formerly presented by demurrer, plea, or answer; and gives option to move to dismiss points of law on the face of the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know which defenses previously cognizable by plea in bar/abatement may be separately heard before trial so parties can avoid unnecessary preparation for trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity pleading must be short, simple, and omit evidence (Equity Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complaint should consist merely of a short and simple statement of the ultimate facts upon which the plaintiff asks relief, omitting any mere statement of evidence, and the answer should in short and simple terms set out the defences, omitting statements of evidence and specifically admitting or denying or explaining the facts set up in the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this brevity requirement, courts provide for bills of particulars to compel amplification where necessary to avoid surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill of particulars: scope and function
rubrics_metrics.description: A further and better statement of the nature of the claim or defence, or further and better particulars of any matter stated in any pleading may be ordered upon such terms as to costs and otherwise as may be just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill of particulars amplifies general allegations to inform the adversary of the precise nature and character of the claim/defence to prevent surprise at trial. It is intended to remedy ignorance of the nature of the claim, not mere ignorance of facts. Courts (e.g., SDNY) have used bills of particulars to require descriptions of inventions/uses and the patents/publications relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to state date(s) of invention (jurisdictional practice varies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a plaintiff should be compelled to fix the date of his invention has been contested: one court (E.D. Pa.) refused as 'an innovation in pleading', while the S.D.N.Y. practice obliges each party to inform the other of the dates of invention they intend to prove, with interchange required to be simultaneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local practice varies; be prepared in jurisdictions like SDNY to disclose the claimed date(s) of invention and any dates relied on to anticipate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill of particulars for prior use/anticipation: contents
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill of particulars of the answer will not be required stating in whose presence an alleged prior use or invention occurred, but a defendant will be required to give a description of the thing(s) invented or used or the ingredients of a composition or manufacture or of a process involved or practiced in its production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defendant may refuse to disclose a secret process; these requirements generally apply only when the defendant sets up prior use/process as an anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of patents/publications relied on for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may be required to name the patents and publications that would be offered in evidence to support the contention of anticipation, and to state of those which he will rely on at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Learned Hand: although statute allows pleading many patents, the number that can serve as true anticipations must be very limited; the court will direct the defendant to declare which patents he seriously contends are anticipations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction for overbroad anticipation lists
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court is satisfied at conclusion that defendants could, without reasonable danger, have cut down the patents on which they rely below the number given in response to the court's order, the court may deprive the defendant of costs or award costs against defendants notwithstanding their success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An order compelling specification of patents/publications must carry an effective sanction (typically costs) to be meaningful; parties should avoid listing excessive or frivolous anticipations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical caution about affidavits and perjury
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive oaths ought to be based on positive knowledge; it is feared many persons make affidavits without much reflection upon the statements or upon the pains and penalties of perjury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawyers should guard the conscience of clients regarding affidavits; ensure affiants understand statements and have requisite knowledge before swearing.
